Rear-view of a car on a banked curve at the design speed — W and N are the only forces acting, and the dashed parallelogram builds their sum: a horizontal net force pointing at the centre of the turn. Ghost cars show what the wrong speed does — too slow slips down the bank, too fast slides up it.

About: The Banked Turn — One Speed the Road Was Built For

Source

Topic
Circular motion — banked road (JEE / NCERT Class 11)
Simulation
Rear view of a car on a banked curve, with force diagram and safe-speed band
Concept
The design speed of a banked turn depends only on radius and bank angle — friction never enters it, it only widens the tolerance band around it.
Serves
Recognising the design speed as a geometric quantity; distinguishing it from the friction-dependent safe range.
Inquiry
Set μ = 0, read the design speed. Predict what happens to that design speed as μ rises, then check.
Misconception
"A banked road has a safe speed, and more friction raises it."

Guided Inquiry

Step 1 — the frictionless case

The friction coefficient has been set to μ = 0. With no friction, only the bank itself can turn the car. Read the design speed off the band beneath the scene, then press Next.

Step 2 — predict

You are about to drag the friction slider μ up from 0. What will happen to the design speed — the speed marked vd on the band?

Step 3 — drag μ and watch

Drag the μ slider from 0 up toward 0.4. Watch the green marker vd on the band — and the two ends of the shaded safe range.

The band widens in both directions. The design speed marker doesn't move.

Step 4 — the whole picture

Now try the speed slider. Below vmin the car slides down the bank (into the turn); above vmax it slides up and off. Between them, static friction closes the gap between the bank's pull and what the turn requires.

Change the bank angle θ. That does move vd — because the design speed is geometry.

01

At a glance

A car drives around a banked bend, drawn as a slice across the road. Three sliders set its speed, the bank angle and the friction, and a band below the road marks the safe speeds.

What you'll learn

  • Which forces turn a car around a banked bend.
  • How the bank angle, the friction and the speed decide whether the car stays on the road.
  • How to find the speeds at which it stays on.
The road is tilted by θ from the horizontal. The car drives into the page, around a bend whose centre lies to the left.

What's on screen

  • N normal force (amber) and W weight (rose), drawn for a 1 kg car.
  • f friction (violet), along the road surface, and Fc required (green, dashed): the inward force the turn needs at the current speed.
  • vd (green) and vmin, vmax (amber): markers on the speed band. A blue pointer marks the car's speed v.

Fixed: radius of the bend r = 50 m and g = 9.81 m/s². The arrows are drawn for a car of mass 1 kg. The speeds below do not depend on the mass.

03

The design speed comes from the bank alone

Take μ = 0. Only two forces act: the weight mg, straight down, and the normal force N, perpendicular to the tilted road. The horizontal part of N points toward the centre of the turn, so it supplies the force the circle needs.

N cosθ = mg  ·  N sinθ = mv²/r
Divide the second by the first: tanθ = v²/(rg), so vd = √(rg tanθ)

The mass cancels. With r = 50 m and θ = 20°, vd = √(50 × 9.81 × 0.364) = 13.36 m/s, about 48 km/h.

With no friction, only vd itself works. At any other speed, nothing balances the mismatch and the car slides. The sim opens at 13.4 m/s, a hair above 13.36, and already shows the car sliding up.

See itSet θ = 20° and μ = 0, and look at the band. Watch for: the green vd marker at 13.36 m/s, the same value as in the readout.
04

Friction widens the safe band on both sides

Static friction acts along the road surface, and its size is at most μN. Below vd it points up the slope, and above vd it points down the slope. At the two ends of the band it is at its limit.

vmin = √( rg (tanθ − μ) / (1 + μ tanθ) )
vmax = √( rg (tanθ + μ) / (1 − μ tanθ) )
μ does not appear in vd = √(rg tanθ), so the green marker stays put.

At θ = 20° and μ = 0.2: vmin = 8.66 m/s, vd = 13.36 m/s and vmax = 17.27 m/s. The band reaches 4.70 m/s below vd and 3.91 m/s above it. Between the ends, friction supplies whatever the bank leaves over.

See itSet θ = 20° and μ = 0.2. Watch for: the green marker staying at 13.36 m/s while the amber vmin and vmax stand at 8.66 and 17.27 m/s.
05

Outside the band the car slides

Below vmin, even the largest friction up the slope cannot stop the car slipping down toward the inside of the turn. Above vmax, even the largest friction down the slope cannot stop it slipping up the bank and off the outer edge.

Take θ = 20° and μ = 0.2, and count forces for each kilogram of the car. At 5 m/s the friction needed is 2.89 N, but the most the tyres give is μN = 1.88 N, so the car slides down. At 25 m/s the friction needed is 8.39 N against 2.70 N, so it slides up and off.

If μ ≥ tanθ, which is 0.364 at 20°, friction alone stops the car slipping down at any speed, so vmin = 0. The sim then labels it "cannot slide down".

See itSet θ = 20° and μ = 0.2, then lower v to 5 m/s. Watch for: the blue pointer left of vmin = 8.66, an amber arrow, and the note saying the car slides down the bank.
06

The bank angle sets the design speed

Because vd = √(rg tanθ), a steeper bank suits a faster car. At r = 50 m: 10° gives 9.30 m/s, 20° gives 13.36 m/s, 30° gives 16.83 m/s and 45° gives 22.15 m/s.

The growth is gentler than it looks: the speed goes as √(tanθ). A larger radius also raises vd, as √r, but r is fixed at 50 m here.

Moving θ moves the whole band: vmin and vmax follow vd up or down.

These numbers follow the sim's sliders.

See itRaise θ to 30° with μ = 0.2. Watch for: the green marker at 16.83 m/s, and the amber ends at 12.88 and 20.76 m/s.
07

Where it matters

  • Highway bends. A bend is banked for a typical speed. Friction covers cars a little faster or slower, and on a wet road a smaller μ narrows the band while vd stays the same.
  • Railway curves. The outer rail is raised, so a train at the design speed needs no sideways push from the rails.
  • Cycle tracks. A steeply banked track lets riders corner fast without relying on grip.
  • Aircraft. A pilot rolls the wings to bank. The horizontal part of the lift then turns the plane, and tanθ = v²/(rg) again links angle and speed.
08

Summary

In one line. The sim shows a car on a banked bend and marks the speeds at which it stays on the road, for the bank angle and friction you choose.

Key points

  • vd = √(rg tanθ): set by the bank and the radius, not by μ or the mass.
  • Friction widens the band: vmin falls and vmax rises as μ grows.
  • Below vmin the car slides down the bank. Above vmax it slides up and off.
  • A steeper bank raises vd and moves the whole band.

Common mix-ups

  • "Better grip raises the design speed." Grip only widens the safe band on both sides of vd.
  • "Fc is an extra force that pushes the car round." Fc = mv²/r is what N and f must add up to, not a new arrow.
  • "A heavier car needs a different speed." The mass cancels from every speed above.

Things to try on your own

  • Set μ = 0 and θ = 10°. Read vd, then check it with √(rg tanθ).
  • At θ = 10°, raise μ until vmin reads 0. Compare that μ with tan 10° = 0.176.
  • At θ = 20° and μ = 0.4, find vmax (20.94 m/s) and push v just past it.
